name: TM25S
desc: The Techman TM25S is the heavy-payload flagship of Techman's TM AI Cobot S Series and, at launch (Automate 2023), claimed the longest reach of any 25 kg-payload cobot — 1,902 mm — paired with a class-leading ±0.03 mm repeatability (a 70% precision gain over the prior generation) and TCP speeds to 5.2 m/s, its 6th-axis joint speed doubled from 225 to 450°/s for a 25% cycle-time cut. What sets Techman apart from every other cobot maker is vision-native design: a 5 MP autofocus camera is built into the arm (eye-in-hand), driving TMvision, AI object recognition and AOI inspection with no add-on vision controller, plus a built-in force/torque sensor at the end for force control. It's programmed through TMflow 2's flow-based graphical nodes — approachable for first-timers — with TMscript for engineers and TMcraft for custom C#/WPF plug-ins, on a TÜV-certified, ISO 10218-1 / ISO/TS 15066 safety base with an IP54 control cabinet and official TM ROS driver.
cameras: Built-in 5 MP autofocus vision system (eye-in-hand) — TMvision, AI object recognition

axes_config: 6-axis AI collaborative arm with built-in vision

name: GoFa 12 (CRB 15000)
desc: The ABB GoFa 12 is the payload flagship of the CRB 15000 collaborative family — 12 kg across 1,270 mm wrist reach (1,370 mm flange) at the line's ±0.02 mm repeatability and 2.2 m/s TCP speed, from a 48 kg IP67-sealed arm that actually undercuts the longer GoFa 10 on mass. It carries the complete GoFa architecture: torque and position sensors in all six joints, PL d Cat. 3 SafeMove power-and-force limiting with up to 16 safety zones, rounded no-pinch geometry, interaction status light, and the OmniCore controller running RobotWare 7. Programming spans grab-anywhere lead-through, Wizard Easy Programming blocks on the FlexPendant, RAPID, and RobotStudio offline with ~99% simulation fidelity; the Ultra Accuracy option brings 0.03 mm path accuracy for sealing and laser work at full payload. ISO Class 4 cleanroom rated, any-direction mounting, Pro variant with PROFINET.
position_accuracy_mm: Ultra Accuracy option: 0.03 mm path / 0.1 mm absolute
ft_sensor: Integrated torque + position sensors in all 6 joints
safety_pl: PL d Cat. 3 (SafeMove Collaborative — up to 16 configurable safety zones)

name: E0509 (E-Series)
desc: The Doosan E0509 is the world's first collaborative robot built exclusively for the food & beverage industry — the sole model of Doosan's E-Series, a 6-axis 5 kg / 900 mm cobot with ±0.05 mm repeatability that is engineered around hygiene rather than adapted from a factory arm. Its NSF (US food-grade) certification and IP66 rating let operators wash it down and maintain hygiene without robot jackets or added equipment, and it ships in a box two-thirds the size of previous Doosan cobots for easy transport and install in cafés, kiosks and food counters. Purpose-built for repeatable service motions — it can pour a hand-drip coffee like a barista (three cups in 15 seconds), handle timing-sensitive cooking steps, and serve — it runs Doosan's DART-Platform software (graphical programming, DRL, Python) on a rugged real-time controller, with TÜV SÜD-certified collision detection for fenceless operation and official ROS/ROS 2 drivers. Doosan cites F&B automation ROI in as little as 14 months. NOTE: distinct model — do not conflate with the general-purpose A0509 (some aggregators merge them).
teach_pendant: DART-Platform (PC/pendant) + safety stop button
ft_sensor: Collision detection via joint current/torque sensing
safety_functions: Intelligent collision detection; safety-rated monitored stop; direct teaching

name: AquaSense 2 Ultra
desc: The Beatbot AquaSense 2 Ultra (CES 2025 flagship) is a cordless robotic pool cleaner covering floor, walls, waterline and water surface. AI HybridSense navigation (27 sensors incl. cameras + ultrasonics) builds a pool map and targets high-debris zones; dual brushes, a 5 L debris basket (150um+250um dual filter), dual LED night cleaning and self-parking at the pool edge. ~3.5 h runtime, 4-5 h charge.
cleaning_coverage: 5-in-1: surface + floor + walls + waterline + water clarification

name: Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus
desc: The Maytronics Dolphin Nautilus CC Plus is a popular corded robotic pool cleaner (~8.6 kg) with dual scrubbing brushes, a large top-load filter, wall-climbing and CleverClean navigation, plus app scheduling on the CC Plus model. 60 ft anti-tangle swivel cable for in-ground pools.
app: None (2019 base; CC Plus Wi-Fi variant exists)

name: S2 Solar
desc: The WYBOT S2 Solar is a solar-powered autonomous surface pool skimmer that floats and continuously collects leaves and debris from the water surface, recharging from the sun for hands-free daily skimming.
battery_type: Rechargeable, with floating solar charging dock

name: HOBOT-S6 Pro
desc: A premium window-cleaning robot from Taiwan's HOBOT (a window-bot pioneer since 2010), and the first with a patented dual-mop reciprocating polish — two cleaning cloths vibrating 600 times a minute over a 4 mm stroke to lift dirt and neutralise static for longer-lasting shine. Dual ultrasonic nozzles atomise water into 15 µm mist (about 1.3 ml per m²) for streak-free cleaning, while Edge-Leakage-Bumper sensors handle framed and frameless glass. Caterpillar treads move at 12 cm/s, cleaning 1 m² in ~2.6 minutes, with a UPS holding position for 20 minutes on power loss.
estop: Anti-falling algorithm + UPS 20 min + 4.5 m safety rope (230 kgf)
power_source: Corded (5 m cable, secure DC jack)

name: Litter-Robot 4
desc: The Whisker Litter-Robot 4 is a self-cleaning automatic litter box that sifts and rotates to separate waste after each use, with OmniSense weight/litter-level sensing that tracks each cat's weight and litter level, reporting to the Whisker app over Wi-Fi.

name: Grillbot
desc: A hand-sized automatic grill-cleaning robot that scrubs a barbecue grill at the push of a button. Three independent motors drive spinning brushes (available in brass, nylon or steel) inside a heat-resistant shell, moving in a random spin-stop-restart pattern for even coverage. An LCD timer offers 10, 20 or 30-minute cycles, and it runs on hot or cold grills. Powered by a rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

name: Tertill
desc: The first robotic weeder for home gardens, created by Roomba co-inventor Joe Jones at Franklin Robotics (later Tertill Corp) in North Billerica, Massachusetts. This solar-powered, weatherproof disc lives in the garden from spring to fall, using capacitive bumper sensors to tell tall plants from short weeds and a spinning nylon string trimmer to cut weeds at the base. Four-wheel drive with extreme camber wheels handles soil, sand and mulch; a physical garden border replaces any perimeter wire or GPS.
use_cases: Home garden weeding (up to ~200 sq ft)

name: Ghost (Anduril sUAS)
desc: Anduril's first drone: a soldier-portable, single-rotor helicopter-style VTOL small UAS built for quiet, modular ISR, targeting and force protection at the tactical edge. Running at low rotor speed for a near-silent acoustic signature, the ~17 kg Ghost 4 carries modular payloads — a Trillium EO/IR gimbal plus optional SIGINT, EW and radar — swappable in seconds, and is driven by Anduril's Lattice AI core (~3.2 TOPS) that enables full autonomy, sub-one-hour operator training, swarming and automatic 'battlefield handover' between aircraft for persistent coverage. Sold in pairs and packable in a backpack or Pelican case, two Ghosts give one operator round-the-clock ISR. The upgraded Ghost-X (2023) adds dual batteries, a tandem-rotor layout, vision-based GPS-denied navigation and far greater payload.
variants: Ghost-X (dual-battery, tandem-rotor, 25 kg MTOW, 75 min, GPS-denied)

name: Ion Endoluminal (Bronchoscopy)
desc: The Intuitive Ion is a robotic endoluminal platform for minimally invasive peripheral lung biopsy, using an ultrathin, maneuverable shape-sensing catheter to navigate deep into the lung for early cancer diagnosis.
use_cases: Robotic bronchoscopy for peripheral lung biopsy

name: 8R Autonomous (driverless)
desc: John Deere's autonomous 8R adds a retrofit autonomy kit (six stereo camera pairs, GPS and onboard AI) to its 8R tractor line, enabling driver-free tillage and field work with remote monitoring and control via a mobile dashboard.
sensing: 6 stereo camera pairs + GPS + onboard AI

name: Guardian XO (full-body exo)
desc: A full-body powered exoskeleton letting a worker lift up to 90 kg as if a fraction of the weight, at ~200:1 amplification. The 24-DoF Guardian XO runs on hot-swappable batteries for continuous shift work.
use_cases: Industrial heavy lifting — logistics, aviation, defense

name: T800
desc: The EngineAI T800 is the company's flagship full-size humanoid (CES 2026 debut, mass production from ~June 2026): ~1.73 m, ~75 kg, 29 body DOF (+7/hand), up to 3 m/s, 450 Nm peak-torque joints, a magnesium-aluminium alloy frame and a notable solid-state battery (~3 h). NVIDIA Jetson compute, 360 deg LiDAR + RealSense. Went viral for fluid martial-arts demos; offered in multiple editions from ~5,000.
note: Flagship; viral martial-arts video (CEO took kick on camera to rebut CGI claims)

name: HMND 01
desc: HMND 01, from London-based startup Humanoid, is a modular next-generation labor-automation humanoid engineered for industrial deployment with an explicit focus on low total cost of ownership. Standing 175 cm and 70 kg with 41 DOF, a 15 kg payload and 1.5 m/s walking speed, its standout trait is manipulation speed — hands that can move faster than a human's, via high-torque, high-speed self-developed actuators. Modularity is central: the upper body, lower body and end-effectors are interchangeable (a 12-DOF five-finger hand or a 1-DOF parallel gripper), and it comes in two Alpha forms — a bipedal version with an RL-trained whole-body controller (walking straight and curved, turning in place, sidestepping, backwards walking, squatting, hopping, running, with omnidirectional push recovery) and an omnidirectional wheeled version (up to 7.2 km/h). It runs Humanoid's KinetIQ framework (VLM + VLA based) for autonomous or teleoperated operation, with RGB plus dual depth cameras, a 6-mic array, and a head display with LEDs for multimodal interaction, and interchangeable protective garments for contamination control. Humanoid completed a bin-picking proof-of-concept with Schaeffler at its Erlangen site. NOTE: full specs from Humanoid official + humanoid.guide/QVIRO — verified; development-stage (Alpha prototypes 2025).

The 165cm models stand 165cm at ≤55kg with 31-33 DOF (6 per leg, 7 per arm, 3 waist, 2 neck); the 175cm flagship reaches 43 DOF, ≤60kg, 250 N·m peak torque, 5kg single-arm payload and a 9-axis IMU. All walk at up to 5 km/h and offer interchangeable end effectors (2-finger 1-DoF gripper, 3-finger 4-DoF gripper, or 5-finger 6-DoF dexterous hand). Compute scales from dual RK3588 (motion control) on the Lite/EDU to added NVIDIA Orin NX (157 TOPS) perception on Super/175cm, with an optional AGX Orin computing backpack (275 TOPS). A 9,500mAh slide-out battery gives ~1.5-2h, and the platform includes head/chest/wrist/hip depth cameras, LiDAR (higher variants), Wi-Fi 6, 5G, gigabit Ethernet, voice interaction, OTA and a full developer API suite (remote-control, sensor, low- and high-level motion control). name: N1
desc: The Fourier N1 (Nexus-01) is billed as the first fully open-source humanoid robot, launched by Shanghai-based Fourier Intelligence in April 2025 along with its complete bill of materials, CAD/STEP drawings, assembly instructions and control software on GitHub. The compact 1.3 m, 38 kg platform has 23 degrees of freedom (excluding hands) in an aluminium-alloy and engineering-plastic frame, driven by Fourier's self-developed FSA 2.0 integrated actuators delivering up to 96 N·m peak joint torque and a top running speed of 3.5 m/s. A back-mounted swappable battery gives 2+ hours of continuous operation. In validation it logged over 1,000 hours of outdoor testing — climbing 15-20° slopes and 20 cm stairs and recovering from falls. As the founding project of Fourier's 'Nexus' open-source ecosystem, the N1 is aimed at researchers, educators and developers as a low-barrier platform for embodied-AI and locomotion R&D.

name: Elektro
desc: Elektro, built by Westinghouse in 1937-39 and starring at the 1939 New York World's Fair, is one of the most famous early humanoid robots — a 2.1-metre (7-foot), ~120 kg gold-finished machine that captured the public imagination decades before modern robotics. Driven by electric motors, relays and photoelectric cells, it could walk on command (triggered by voice through a telephone-style link that converted words to relay pulses), speak a roughly 700-word vocabulary played from 78-rpm records, move its arms and head, count on its fingers, distinguish red and green light via photocells, and even 'smoke' a cigarette. It appeared with a robot dog, Sparko. Though it was a showcase automaton rather than an autonomous robot, Elektro is a landmark in the cultural and engineering history of humanoids. name: Unimate
desc: The Unimate is the world's first industrial robot — conceived by George Devol (who patented 'Programmed Article Transfer' in 1954) and commercialised by Joseph Engelberger through Unimation, with the first unit installed on a General Motors die-casting line in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961. A roughly 1,800 kg hydraulic arm with polar-coordinate motion (~5 axes) and a magnetic-drum memory that stored taught positions, it could lift heavy die-cast parts (payloads into the hundreds of kilograms) and perform spot welding on automobile bodies — dangerous, repetitive jobs it took over from human workers. The Unimate launched the entire industrial-robotics industry, made GM assembly lines the proving ground for automation, and led directly to Unimation's later PUMA. NOTE: The Unimate predates modern spec documentation; figures here reflect the historical record (payload ~227 kg / ~500 lb class, hydraulic drive, magnetic-drum control) and are intentionally limited to verified historical facts rather than a reconstructed datasheet.

name: Shakey
desc: The first mobile robot that could reason about its own actions (1966–72). Shakey perceived its world with a TV camera and bump sensors, planned with the STRIPS algorithm, and rerouted around obstacles — work that produced A* search, computer vision foundations and modern AI planning.

name: WABOT-1
desc: WABOT-1, completed in 1973 at Waseda University under Professor Ichiro Kato ('father of Japanese robotics'), is recognised as the world's first full-scale anthropomorphic (humanoid) robot — the machine that began the entire quest to build robots in human form. It integrated, for the first time in one platform, quasi-static bipedal walking (keeping its centre of mass inside the support polygon), object grasping and transport with human-finger-mimicking hands, a stereo-camera vision system that measured distance and direction to objects, and a conversation system that recognised and responded to simple spoken Japanese through an artificial voice. Researchers compared its overall ability to that of a 1½-year-old child. Hydraulically driven and slow, it could only walk on flat surfaces — but it proved humanoid robots were possible and jump-started the field worldwide. It's on public display at Waseda's Nishi-Waseda campus. name: WABOT-2
desc: WABOT-2, introduced in 1984 by Waseda University's Kato laboratory, was the world's first musician humanoid robot — a 50-degrees-of-freedom machine that could read a printed musical score with its CCD-camera head and play a Yamaha FX-1 electronic keyboard using both hands and feet, even adjusting its performance to accompany a human singer. Its five-fingered hands with 3-DOF fingers performed precise, delicate keypresses, driven by DC motors and harmonic drives. Its distributed computing was remarkable for 1984: a 16-bit Zilog Z8001 for high-level limb control, two Z8002s for mid-level control while playing, and fifty 8-bit Z8094 CPUs — one dedicated to each degree of freedom — for low-level motor control. WABOT-2 demonstrated that humanoids could perform artistic, dexterous, real-time tasks, not just walk. name: Stanford Cart
desc: A pioneering self-driving vehicle research platform. In its famous 1979 run under Hans Moravec, the Cart crossed a chair-filled room entirely autonomously in about five hours, using stereo TV vision processed by a remote mainframe — ancestral DNA of every modern autonomous vehicle.

name: PUMA 560
desc: The PUMA 560 (Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly) is one of the most historically important industrial robots ever built — developed by Victor Scheinman at Unimation in 1978, together with General Motors, and considered the archetypal anthropomorphic robot arm. Its six all-rotational axes with a 3R spherical wrist (2.5 kg payload, 864 mm reach, ~±0.1 mm repeatability, DC servos under Unimation's VAL controller) made it the reference manipulator for a generation of robotics research: its kinematics and Denavit-Hartenberg parameters appear in countless textbooks, and it remained a laboratory and teaching standard for decades. It shipped in a family (PUMA 260, 560, 761) and cemented Unimation — founded by robotics pioneer Joseph Engelberger — as the birthplace of industrial robotics. NOTE: The PUMA predates modern datasheet practice; specifications here are drawn from the published academic and historical record (Unimation documentation, robotics literature) rather than a current manufacturer datasheet — depth is intentionally capped to verified historical figures rather than invented.
actuator_type: DC servo motors with encoders (VAL controller)

name: Skilam SCARA
desc: The Sankyo Seiki Skilam is one of the first commercial SCARA robots — the SCARA concept (Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm) was invented by Professor Hiroshi Makino at the University of Yamanashi around 1978-1981, and Sankyo Seiki was among the pioneering manufacturers (with the Makino lab) to commercialise it as the Skilam line. The SCARA's defining trait is selective compliance: rigid in the vertical (Z) axis but compliant in the horizontal plane, making it ideal for vertical insertion and assembly tasks — peg-in-hole, screwdriving, electronics placement — at high speed. This 4-axis architecture (two horizontal rotary joints, a vertical Z, and end rotation) became one of the two dominant industrial-robot form factors worldwide, and virtually every modern SCARA (Epson, Stäubli TS2, Denso, Yamaha) descends from this lineage. NOTE: The original Skilam predates modern datasheet publication; this entry documents the historically verified milestone and architecture rather than inventing per-axis figures — specific payload/reach numbers for the original model are logged as outreach rather than guessed.
actuator_type: Servo-driven horizontal articulated arm + vertical Z + rotation

name: HERO 1
desc: One of the earliest consumer/educational robots — the Heathkit Educational RObot (model ET-18), begun in 1979 and released in 1982, sold as a build-it-yourself kit ($1,500) or assembled ($2,500) with ~14,000+ units shipped. HERO 1 is a self-contained mobile robot on a Motorola 6808 8-bit CPU (1 MHz) with 4 KB RAM and 8 KB ROM, driven by seven stepper motors plus a DC drive motor across a three-wheel base whose head rotates 350 degrees to aim its sensors and optional arm. Onboard light, sound, ultrasonic-motion and Polaroid sonar sensors, an optical encoder and a real-time clock let it perceive its world; an optional five-axis arm/gripper and Votrax SC-01 speech synthesizer added manipulation and voice. Programmed in 6808 machine code via a 17-key hex keypad, a record/replay Teaching Pendant, or an IBM-PC ANDROTEXT compiler, with cassette-tape program storage. It even starred on TV's 'Mr. Wizard's World'.

name: RB5X
desc: A cylindrical, R2-D2-esque personal robot from RB Robot Corporation (Golden, Colorado; founded by Joe Bosworth in 1982) — one of the earliest commercial autonomous mobile robots and among the most durable personal robots of the 1980s (still manufactured today by RB Robotics). Under a clear domed top, RB5X runs a National INS8073 microprocessor with on-chip TinyBASIC and 8K of memory (expandable to 16K), programmable in TinyBASIC or Savvy and downloadable from any home computer over its (dual) RS-232 interface. It rolls at ~4 in/sec on two drive wheels and two casters, sensing the world with eight perimeter bump panels, a photodiode and a Polaroid sonar rangefinder (10 in to 35 ft). It learns from experience, finds its own charging nest when low, and offers an optional five-axis arm (lifts ~1 lb) and voice synthesizer. Sold in Germany as 'Toby'.

name: Armatron
desc: An iconic early-1980s robotic-arm toy from Tomy that introduced a generation to robotics and mechanical engineering. Entirely mechanical — a single electric motor drives an intricate gear train — it is operated by two joysticks that command multiple simultaneous motions: base rotation, shoulder and elbow articulation, wrist rotation and a grasping claw. A built-in countdown timer challenged users to complete pick-and-place tasks, and it ran on batteries with no electronics or programming. A celebrated example of purely mechanical multi-axis control.
actuator_type: Single electric motor + mechanical gear train

name: Omnibot
desc: An iconic 1980s programmable home robot from Japanese toymaker Tomy. Using a built-in cassette-tape deck, Omnibot could record and play back sequences of movements and speech, letting owners program it to roll around, speak and serve drinks from its front tray. It featured a wheeled base, remote control and a built-in clock/alarm, and became one of the most recognisable consumer robots of the personal-robot craze.

name: Genghis
desc: Rodney Brooks’ six-legged insect robot that changed robotics philosophy: no world model, no central planner — just layered "subsumption architecture" behaviors that let a 1 kg machine scramble over rough terrain. Its DNA lives on in every behavior-based robot since.

name: Cog
desc: Cog was a landmark embodied-AI research humanoid built by Rodney Brooks's group at the MIT AI Lab from 1994 — an upper-body robot (torso, head, two arms; ~22 DOF on a fixed base) created to test a radical hypothesis: that human-like intelligence can only emerge from a human-like body interacting with the world, not from disembodied computation. Cog had foveated saccading stereo-camera eyes, vestibular and auditory sensing, and joint force sensing (an early platform for series-elastic actuation), and it learned behaviours like reaching, orienting to stimuli and rudimentary social interaction. It was hugely influential — a training ground for researchers including Cynthia Breazeal (who built the expressive robot Kismet nearby) — and shaped the embodied-cognition and social-robotics movements. Notably, Brooks went on to co-found iRobot and later Rethink Robotics (Baxter/Sawyer). NOTE: historic research entry from MIT records — verified specifics; some exact figures (mass, precise DOF by generation) vary and are flagged, not invented.

name: Dante II
desc: The volcano explorer. In 1994 the eight-legged, tether-rappelling Dante II descended into Alaska’s active Mt. Spurr crater to sample fumarole gases too dangerous for humans — a foundational mission for extreme-environment and planetary robotics.

name: P2
desc: Honda's P2, unveiled December 1996, is one of the most important robots in history — the world's first self-regulating, autonomous, wireless bipedal humanoid, and the machine that stunned the robotics world and launched the modern humanoid era. At 1,820 mm and 210 kg with 30 degrees of freedom, it was the first to build everything — computer, motor drives, battery, and wireless radio — into its own torso, freeing it from tethers. It could walk autonomously at 2 km/h, climb up and down stairs (using a six-axis force sensor in its feet to estimate tread depth), push carts, and tighten bolts via a force-reflecting master arm. P2 directly led to ASIMO four years later, was recognised as an IEEE Milestone in 2026, and was loaned to Japan's AIST in 1998 to kick-start the national Humanoid Robotics Project (HRP). NOTE: specs from Honda's official robotics history and the IEEE Milestone record — this is a historic entry documented to verified figures, not a current datasheet.

name: P3
desc: Honda's P3, completed September 1997, is considered the world's first completely independent (fully self-contained) bipedal humanoid walking robot — the final prototype before ASIMO. Honda shrank it substantially from the P2: 1,600 mm and 130 kg (down from 210 kg) with 28 degrees of freedom, achieved by revising component materials and adopting a distributed control system, bringing it closer to a size that could blend into human living spaces. It walked autonomously at 2 km/h, climbed stairs, and pushed carts. The P3 was the direct bridge to ASIMO (2000), and its lineage also seeded AIST's HRP-1. NOTE: figures from Honda's official robotics history; historic entry documented to verified specs, not a modern datasheet.

name: Kismet
desc: A landmark of social robotics built in the late 1990s at MIT by Dr. Cynthia Breazeal as an experiment in affective computing — a robot head that could recognise and simulate emotion. Kismet perceives auditory, visual and proprioceptive social cues and responds with human-readable expressions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise, interest, calm, tiredness) through movements of its ears, eyebrows, eyelids, lips and jaw, plus expressive 'proto-speech' babble and tone of voice. Its active-vision system has four DoF (each eye pans independently, with a shared tilt), and the whole platform runs ~21 actuators fed by four cameras and three microphones across a network of computers. Funded by NTT and DARPA, Kismet now resides at the MIT Museum.

name: Furby
desc: The 1998 Furby — an owl/hamster-like animatronic toy from Tiger Electronics (designed by Dave Hampton and Caleb Chung) that became a cultural phenomenon, selling over 40 million units in three years. About 11 inches tall in synthetic fur, it produced 300+ movement combinations — blinking eyes, wiggling ears, an opening beak and a rocking body — all from a single motor driven through a camshaft gear assembly, a clever cost-saving feat for its time. A 6502-class microprocessor with only 128 bytes of RAM ran everything. Light, sound and touch sensors (in a touch > sound > light hierarchy) plus a tilt sensor let it react to its environment, and an infrared port between its eyes let two Furbies 'talk'. It started out speaking only 'Furbish' (42 root words forming 300+ phrases) and appeared to 'learn' English through play — a simulated effect, not real machine learning.
actuator_type: Single motor + camshaft (eyes, ears, beak, body)

name: MINDSTORMS RCX
desc: The brick that launched LEGO Mindstorms in September 1998 and effectively created the mass-market home-robotics kit. The RCX (Robotic Command eXplorer) grew out of a long LEGO / MIT Media Lab collaboration inspired by Seymour Papert's 'Mindstorms', and shipped as the heart of the Robotics Invention System (RIS 1.0, $199). The yellow programmable brick runs a Renesas H8/300 microcontroller (16 MHz) with 32 KB ROM and 32 KB RAM, exposing three sensor input ports and three 9V motor output ports plus an LCD. Programs are written on a PC (visual RCX Code, or community languages like NQC and leJOS Java) and beamed over infrared; two bricks can even talk to each other via IR. It anchored the first FIRST LEGO League season and built a huge hacker/education community before the line ended in 2022.

desc: The first AIBO — Sony’s entertainment robot dog sold out its initial 3,000 Japanese units in 20 minutes in May 1999. With 18 joints, a camera nose and learned behaviors, ERS-110 created the consumer robot-companion category and remains a design icon.

name: PaPeRo
desc: NEC's 'Partner-type Personal Robot' — a cute, toddler-sized companion robot developed from 1997 (as the R100 prototype) and named PaPeRo in 2001, one of the earliest robots built purely around the human-machine interface rather than locomotion or labour. Standing 385 mm and weighing 5 kg on a three-wheel base, it roams the home looking for faces using twin CCD-camera 'eyes' with facial recognition (identifying ~10 people), then starts a conversation. Four microphones let it locate and understand speech (recognising ~650 commands and speaking ~3,000 phrases), nine capacitance touch sensors sense patting and stroking, and ultrasonic, floor, lift and bumper sensors handle navigation. An expressive LED face (in eyes, mouth, cheeks and ears), stereo speakers, a wireless modem and TV/cellphone links round it out. Never sold publicly, PaPeRo ran for years in NEC's eldercare and smart-home experiments and spawned Childcare, PaPeRo 2005, Mini and Petit variants.

name: QRIO
desc: Sony's compact entertainment humanoid (originally the SDR-4X II prototype), announced in September 2003 as a successor to the AIBO robot dog. At 58 cm and ~7 kg with 38 degrees of freedom, QRIO used ZMP control to walk, dance and recognise faces, and in 2003 became the world's first humanoid capable of sustained running (~23 cm/s) — a feat recognised by Guinness World Records in 2005. It could also recover from falls. Sony ended the project in 2006.

A ~2.7 m, 500 kg high-strength-alloy machine with a roll-cage torso cockpit, it walks upright on two legs, then folds its limbs and shifts its centre of gravity to crawl as a quadruped in seconds, with no external assistance. In the reveal video, CEO Wang Xingxing piloted it as it punched through a brick wall; notably it's optionally manned (runs manned or unmanned/remote). Drawing instant Transformers/Avatar-AMP-suit comparisons, it's pitched as short-range transport, search-and-rescue and demonstration platform. From ¥3.9M (~US$574k–650k), launched alongside Unitree's Shanghai STAR Market IPO. Unitree issued a safety notice cautioning that the platform is early-stage and not for hazardous personal experimentation.

desc: The Elephant Robotics myCobot 280 is recognised by the IEEE as one of the world's smallest six-axis robot arms — an 800-gram desktop cobot with 250 g payload across a 280 mm working radius at ±0.5 mm positioning accuracy, and arguably the most influential education arm of its generation with over 10,000 units sold in 50+ countries. Its controller is built into the base — an M5Stack ESP32 in the standard model or a Raspberry Pi 4 in the Pi variant (860 g), with Arduino and Jetson Nano versions extending the family — so it runs from a 12 V USB-C supply with no cabinet. Programming spans Python via the open-source pymycobot API, Blockly, Arduino and official ROS/ROS 2 packages with MoveIt configs, and an ecosystem of grippers, suction pumps, camera flanges, AI vision kits and the myAGV mobile base builds it into full teaching cells. Official rated working lifespan is 500 hours, reflecting its education-class positioning.

Like its smaller sibling it packs the controller into the base — M5Stack or Raspberry Pi 4 depending on variant — and runs the same open software stack: Python through the open-source pymycobot API, Blockly's graphical interface for beginners, C++ and ROS. The end-effector ecosystem is its practical strength: adaptive grippers, a compressor-driven air parallel gripper for heavier grips, suction pumps and camera flanges mount to the standard interface, supported by AI vision kits for machine-learning coursework. It slots into Elephant's broader platform alongside the myAGV mobile base for mobile-manipulation teaching. Elephant's full parameter table for the 320 (weight, repeatability, joint speeds) lives in its GitBook docs — flagged for a part-2 top-up.

It pairs a mobile wheeled base with adjustable lift mechanics so its arms can work at varying heights, and runs CASBOT's embodied-intelligence architecture (a hierarchical end-to-end plus reinforcement-learning stack with cloud and edge compute) fed by vision, IMU, microphone-array and force/torque sensing. It's the wheeled sibling to CASBOT's bipedal CASBOT 01 ('Wednesday', 1.79 m / 60 kg / 52 DOF / 550 TOPS). Its human-like upper body mimics human arm motion for dexterous tasks while a wheeled base ensures reliable indoor travel, and adjustable-height mechanics let its arms work at different levels — the now-common 'wheeled mobile manipulator' architecture also seen in Galbot G1, CASBOT W1 and RobotEra Q5. name: FF Futurist
desc: The FF Futurist is a full-size professional humanoid from Faraday Future's robotics subsidiary (FF EAI-Robotics), launched in early 2026 as the EV maker's pivot into embodied AI and billed as a candidate to be the first US humanoid in mass production. The 2026 'All-New Futurist' revision stands about 1.73 m and weighs roughly 55 kg, with 31 degrees of freedom (excluding hands), 320 N·m peak knee torque, a top running speed near 11 mph and a 1,152 Wh dual-battery system giving up to six hours of runtime with auto-charging. It runs a VLA + World Model 'brain' on NVIDIA's Sonic motion-control system (Jetson Thor on the Ultra), supports up to 50 languages, and targets reception, guided-service, and light industrial roles. Pricing starts around $34,990.

It offers autonomous patrol and follow-me operation, peak joint torque of 48 N·m, can clear obstacles around 13 inches and climb 40-degree slopes, and supports Wi-Fi and 5G. The platform is modular — an optional four-wheeled version is available, and it can be expanded with LiDAR, depth cameras, robotic arms and security plug-ins. It became one of the first FF robots to clear full US FCC compliance certification, with pricing starting around $2,499.

name: Baxter
cameras: Head camera + cameras in each hand; sonar head sensors; IR hand ranging (Research Robot model)
actuator_type: Series Elastic Actuators (SEA) — spring at every joint absorbs impact & enables back-drive
desc: Rethink Robotics' Baxter (2012) was a landmark in collaborative robotics — the robot that popularised the idea of a fenceless, teach-by-demonstration arm that ordinary factory workers could program by grabbing and moving it. Designed by iRobot co-founder Rodney Brooks, it has a humanoid form: two 7-DOF arms (2.2 kg payload, 1,210 mm reach), a torso, and an animated LCD face that signals intent. Its defining technology is the Series Elastic Actuator — a spring at every joint that both senses force and physically absorbs impact, letting it work safely alongside people without cages under ISO 10218, and back-drive easily when pushed. It runs Intera on ROS from a PC in its chest, with cameras and sensors in its head and hands. The Research Robot variant (added head camera, sonar, IR, and an open SDK) became a fixture in university labs worldwide and seeded a generation of manipulation research. Priced around US$25,000, Baxter is discontinued (Rethink ceased operations in 2018, the brand later acquired), but its influence on cobot design endures. NOTE: Rethink published limited formal spec tables; figures here are from Rethink materials and the Baxter Research Robot documentation.

desc: Rethink Robotics' Sawyer (2015) was the more precise, single-arm successor to Baxter — a 7-DOF collaborative arm weighing just 19 kg with a 4 kg payload, 1,260 mm reach, and ±0.1 mm repeatability, designed to fit into work cells built for humans and reach where the larger dual-arm Baxter couldn't. Rethink redesigned its signature Series Elastic Actuators with a titanium spring and added Harmonic Drive servos and zero-backlash gearboxes, so Sawyer could 'feel' its way into fixtures and machines even when part positions varied slightly — the compliant-motion 'adaptive repeatability' that set Rethink apart. An embedded Cognex vision camera in the arm powers its Robot Positioning System for quick reorientation and redeployment, and it programs by zero-force hand guiding or the Intera 5 visual environment, on ROS with an open SDK. Certified ISO 10218-1 / PL d Cat. 3 for fenceless use and priced around US$29,000, Sawyer targeted machine tending, circuit-board testing and electronics assembly. Discontinued after Rethink ceased operations in 2018; the brand and Sawyer line were subsequently acquired and relaunched.

BigDog could carry ~150 kg over rough terrain, ice and slopes, famously staying upright when kicked. Loud and never deployed, but its dynamic-balance research directly led to Spot and the modern quadruped industry.

name: Cheetah 3

Using high-torque backdriveable electric motors and pure proprioception — no cameras — Cheetah 3 climbs stairs, recovers from shoves and runs ~3 m/s. Successor to the 6 m/s tethered MIT Cheetah; its actuator design seeded Mini Cheetah and much of modern legged robotics.

name: Mini Cheetah
desc: A 9 kg agile quadruped from MIT (2019) — the first robot of its kind to do a backflip. Built from low-cost custom modular actuators, designed to survive high-impact falls and operate upside-down, MIT built a pack of them for distributed locomotion research. Hugely influential on the affordable-quadruped wave.

name: HRP-4C (Miim)
frame_material: Silicone face/hands, plastic exterior, metal frame
desc: HRP-4C, nicknamed Miim, is AIST's landmark entertainment humanoid — an adult-size female android unveiled in 2009, proportioned to the average young Japanese woman (per the 1997-98 Japanese body-dimension database) at 1,600 mm and 43 kg including battery. Its realism was its point: a silicone-skinned face driven by 8 dedicated facial-expression motors on top of 30 body motors (44 DOF total), speech recognition and ambient-sound awareness, and Vocaloid-powered singing. Miim walked using the HRP series' proven gait control, sang and danced alongside human performers with motion-capture-driven movement, and even worked as a professional robotic fashion model — her first gig modelling a wedding dress in 2009. She later served in evaluating nursing-care equipment. HRP-4C became a global symbol of Japan's lead in expressive, human-like humanoids. name: Geminoid F
actuator_type: 12 pneumatic actuators (vs 50 on Geminoid HI-1 — efficient facial design)

desc: Geminoid F ('F' for female), unveiled in 2010 by roboticist Hiroshi Ishiguro (ATR and Osaka University) with animatronics firm Kokoro, is one of the world's most famous ultra-realistic androids — a copy of a real woman in her twenties, with silicone skin and real human hair over a fiber-reinforced-plastic skull. Its design breakthrough was efficiency: where the earlier Geminoid HI-1 (Ishiguro's own copy) used about 50 actuators and a large external compressor box, Geminoid F achieves a convincing 'toothy' smile and a frown with just 12 pneumatic actuators concentrated in the face. It autonomously breathes and blinks, but to fully 'come alive' it's teleoperated: motion-capture software tracks a human operator's facial expressions and head movements and mimics them on the android in real time. It cannot walk — it's always seated — and exists to study human-robot interaction and the nature of 'human presence,' even appearing in theatre productions. It sits within Ishiguro's celebrated android family (Geminoid HI series, Repliee Q1/Q2, Telenoid, Erica). NOTE: specs from IEEE Spectrum + Ishiguro Lab primary sources — museum-grade; recorded honestly as a seated teleoperated android, not a walking biped.

Originating from a DARPA/university collaboration (~2001) and commercialized as the all-terrain X-RHex; a foundational bio-inspired legged-locomotion platform.

desc: Nadine, unveiled in 2015 at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, is a lifelike social android modelled on Professor Nadia Magnenat Thalmann — a pioneer of 'virtual humans' who directed NTU's Institute for Media Innovation and founded the University of Geneva's MIRALab. Its realistic hardware (silicone skin, articulated hands for natural grasping) was built by Japanese animatronics firm Kokoro, while Thalmann's NTU team created the software that gives Nadine her defining qualities: a personality and emotional range, the ability to make eye contact and shake hands, and — unusually — a memory that lets her recognise people she's met and recall previous conversations. Designed as a receptionist or a social companion for people with special needs and the elderly, Nadine became a widely-cited example of socially intelligent androids, conceptually akin to Ishiguro's Geminoids in being modelled on its own creator. name: Keepon
desc: A small yellow snowman-shaped social robot (Hideki Kozima) designed to study social development with children, including autism-therapy research. Its minimal 4-DoF design conveys attention and emotion expressively; the bouncing 'Dancing Keepon' became a viral sensation and a retail toy.

name: Poppy
desc: Poppy, created by INRIA's Flowers team in Bordeaux (born 2012 out of Matthieu Lapeyre's PhD under Pierre-Yves Oudeyer, funded by an ERC grant), is the first complete open-source, 3D-printed humanoid robot — a platform designed so scientists, students, engineers and artists can fast and flexibly explore robot morphologies. About 840 mm tall and only ~3.5 kg, it has 25 DOF driven by Robotis Dynamixel servos, including a distinctive 5-DOF articulated trunk that gives it lumbar-spine-like motion unusual among humanoids. Both hardware (Creative Commons, 3D-printed skeleton, Arduino/Raspberry-Pi electronics) and software (GPL, the Python PyPot library plus a Snap block-based web interface, with V-REP simulation) are fully open, so its mechanical design can be freely modified — it was even reproduced in a two-day workshop at a Paris science museum. Widely adopted in schools and universities across science, education and art, Poppy's compliant Dynamixel control enables soft, safe human-robot interaction. The team later spun out Pollen Robotics, creators of the Reachy open-source humanoid torso. name: Thymio
desc: A small, affordable open-source educational robot from Switzerland (EPFL/Mobsya). With many sensors and colour-coded preprogrammed behaviours, Thymio teaches coding from visual blocks up to Python — a classroom staple across Europe for introducing children to robotics.

Packs a 4K Sony camera, 3D Occipital depth sensor, twin IR cameras, 8 time-of-flight + 6 bump sensors, a 4.3-inch LCD face and an expandable 'backpack' (Arduino). Does SLAM mapping, face/object recognition and autonomous self-charging out of the box. Spun out of Sphero; from $2,399. Acquired by Furhat Robotics in 2022.

desc: A conversational social-robot head that back-projects an animated, fully customizable face onto a 3-DoF moving head. Born from KTH (Stockholm) social-robotics research; named after a fur hat used to hide early prototype wires. Tracks up to 10 people via stereo vision, supports 120+ languages and 200+ voices, and runs the FurhatAI platform (LLM-swappable) with <200ms turn-taking. The most expressive social robot in research/enterprise HRI; from ~$15,000. Acquired Misty Robotics in 2022.

name: VR-H3
desc: The VR-H3, from VinRobotics (a subsidiary of Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup), is the company's third-generation industrial humanoid — a pioneer of Vietnam's entry into industrial humanoids, unveiled at ICRA 2026 in Vienna and COMPUTEX Taipei 2026. Standing about 178 cm and 75-85 kg, it uses more than 31 smart motors driving rotary joints that mimic human kinematics for fluid walking, gesturing and object manipulation in crowded or hazardous factory environments, with each arm lifting around 3 kg. Two onboard edge computers process sensory and operational data locally for low-latency autonomous control, its bipedal locomotion is trained via reinforcement learning with bio-inspired gait design, domain randomization and curriculum learning, and swappable batteries support continuous operation. VinRobotics developed the key technologies in-house — mechanical structure, computing platform, battery management, electrical architecture and AI control software — and demonstrated VR-headset teleoperation with built-in motion capture requiring no external trackers. NOTE: specs from VinRobotics official + ICRA 2026 coverage — verified; development-stage prototype.

name: D1
desc: The D1 from Hong Kong's Direct Drive Technology is billed as the world's first fully modular embodied-intelligence robot. Two wheel-legged biped units (24.3 kg each) dock via a central magnetic coupler to form a 48.6 kg wheel-legged quadruped 'robot dog', then separate again autonomously - a capability the company calls 'All-Domain Splicing'. Each unit runs an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX (8 GB) on Ubuntu 22.04, powered by a 43.2 V / 9 Ah battery good for over five hours, and can roll at up to 11 km/h or walk over rough terrain. Combined, the quadruped carries up to 100 kg (80 kg when standing), with a 25 km empty-load range, targeting security patrol, last-mile delivery, search-and-rescue and mobile filming. A single biped unit is US$7,499; the two-unit quadruped is US$13,999.

name: TORA-ONE
desc: TORA-ONE is a wheeled humanoid robot from Shenzhen-based PaXini Tech, a tactile-sensing specialist backed by a 100-million-yuan strategic investment from BYD. Built around PaXini's 6D Hall-array tactile technology, it carries roughly 1,956 tactile sensors (7,824 channels) alongside five RGB monocular cameras, two depth cameras, fisheye vision and LiDAR with laser SLAM. With an adjustable height of 1.46-1.86 m, 47 degrees of freedom (21 in the body, 26 across its four-fingered bionic hands), plus or minus 0.05 mm arm-positioning accuracy and up to 8 kg per arm, it targets precision assembly, logistics, healthcare and service tasks. TORA-ONE debuted at CES 2026 demonstrating autonomous workflows from ice-cream making to pallet handling, and runs about eight hours per charge.

name: U1 Pro
desc: The UBTech U1 Pro is the first product under UWORLD, UBTech's new consumer sub-brand, billed as the world's first full-size ultra-bionic humanoid built for emotional companionship rather than physical labour. Shipping in male (183 cm / 42 kg) and female (168 cm / 35.2 kg) variants, both with 88 degrees of freedom, it wraps a humanoid frame in lifelike silicone skin with realistic hair, expressive facial actuators and camera-tracking eyes. An on-board emotion-aware AI reads mood from facial expression, tone and speech rhythm and adapts its conversation, with all personal memory stored locally and encrypted; owners can customise appearance and personality over time. Capabilities are deliberately narrow — it can stand, sit and walk on flat indoor surfaces but is not built for stairs, rough terrain, chores, or custom programming. Pre-orders opened on JD.com in June 2026 (passing 2,000+ reservations within days) ahead of a June 30 launch, with deliveries due by September; pricing is reported around US$30,000.
manufacturer_history: U1 Series — human-centred humanoid with locally-encrypted memory and appearance customisation; UBTECH's 2026 consumer-facing line.
