note: Tencent Robotics X lab platform (research, not sold)

name: Sirius
desc: Consumer robot dog with musculoskeletal proprietary joints giving lifelike, springy motion — crowdfunded at about US$1,399 as one of the most agile petbots in its price class.
form_factor: Compact consumer robot dog (musculoskeletal Neurocore joints)
note: Kickstarter consumer agility dog

name: Bittle
desc: Palm-sized open-source robot dog (~290 g) built on the OpenCat framework — Arduino/Raspberry Pi programmable, back-flipping, and hugely popular in STEM education and maker communities.
sdk: OpenCat open-source framework; Arduino/RPi; Python/block coding
use_cases_note: STEM education, hobbyist robotics
note: Kickstarter hit; OpenCat ecosystem

name: Bittle X
desc: An open-source, palm-sized programmable robot dog built on Petoi's OpenCat framework. Powered by an ESP32 controller with 9 servo-driven joints, it walks, trots and does tricks, and is programmable via block-based coding, Arduino/C++ or a Python API. A Raspberry Pi can be mounted for advanced AI and vision projects.

name: CORLEO
desc: A hydrogen-powered, rideable robotic-horse concept unveiled at Expo 2025 Osaka, blending Kawasaki's motorcycle DNA with legged robotics. Four independently articulating legs with slip-resistant split rubber hooves are driven by electricity from a compact 150cc hydrogen engine; the rider steers by shifting weight and using handlebars. The Expo prototype can stand and adjust posture — dynamic footage is CGI — with a market vision decades out.
power_source: Hydrogen engine (generates electricity for leg drives)
form_factor: Rideable four-legged 'horse' concept (rider steers by weight shift)
note: Osaka Expo 2025 showcase — 2050 mobility vision; CGI-heavy reveal, working prototype shown statically

name: Bex
desc: A rideable, goat-inspired quadruped unveiled at the 2022 International Robot Exhibition in Tokyo, part of Kawasaki's Robust Humanoid Platform (RHP) initiative — the same program behind the Kaleido humanoid. Bex walks on four legs or rolls on retractable knee wheels, has a modular upper body, and is aimed at cargo carrying on farms and construction sites.
form_factor: Ibex-inspired RIDEABLE quadruped (kneels to wheel-drive mode)
note: iREX 2022 concept — walks on legs, drives on wheels when kneeling

name: CyberDog
desc: Xiaomi's first robot dog: an open developer platform priced at just 9,999 RMB (~US$1,540) with NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX brain and 3.2 m/s top speed — the machine that kicked off China's cheap-quadruped race.
camera: AI interactive + binocular ultra-wide + Intel RealSense D450 depth
note: Xiaomi's open-source quadruped debut

name: aibo ERS-1000
desc: Sony's beloved aibo reborn: the 2018 ERS-1000 with OLED eyes, 22 actuated axes, cloud-linked AI personality that develops uniquely with its owner, and fish-eye + SLAM cameras. ~US$2,899.
note: AIBO revival — develops unique personality via cloud AI

name: AIBO ERS-7
desc: The third and final generation of Sony's original AIBO line and the first the company explicitly called a 'robot dog'. Featuring the Illume-Face LED array, capacitive touch sensors and MIND software with self-charging, face recognition and name memory, it was widely adopted in academic research and served as the RoboCup Standard Platform League robot from 2004 to 2008.

name: ANYmal C
desc: The quadruped that proved autonomous industrial inspection: ~50 kg, IP67, self-charging ANYmal C ran routine inspections on offshore platforms and plants worldwide before being succeeded by ANYmal D.
use_cases_note: Autonomous industrial inspection (oil & gas, energy) — ETH heritage
note: Full autonomous-mission stack (docking, routine inspection)

name: ANYmal X
desc: The explosion-proof member of the ANYmal family, certified for hazardous (Ex) zones such as oil, gas and chemical plants. Built on the ANYmal D platform with an Ex-rated sealed housing, it performs fully autonomous inspection in potentially explosive atmospheres where other legged robots cannot operate. Shares the D platform's dual-Intel compute, 360° LiDAR navigation and pan-tilt inspection payload.

name: LittleDog
desc: A small DARPA-funded research quadruped built by Boston Dynamics as a standard testbed platform for other institutions studying rough-terrain locomotion and machine learning. Each of its four legs is driven by three electric motors, with an onboard PC handling sensing, control and communications.
note: Standard learning-locomotion testbed used by MIT/Stanford/CMU/USC teams

name: WildCat
desc: The untethered, free-roaming successor to Cheetah, developed under DARPA's M3 program. Powered by an onboard methanol combustion engine driving hydraulic actuators, WildCat bounded and galloped outdoors at up to 25.7 km/h — the fastest untethered legged robot of its era.
speed: ~32 km/h free-running (untethered outdoor record of its era)
note: Untethered successor to Cheetah — galloping + bounding gaits

name: Cheetah
desc: A DARPA-funded (Maximum Mobility and Manipulation program) research quadruped that set the legged-robot land-speed record, hitting 45 km/h on a laboratory treadmill. Tethered and boom-stabilised, with an articulated spine that flexed each stride to extend its gallop. Its untethered successor was WildCat.
speed: 45.5 km/h — treadmill land-speed record for legged robots (2012, beat Usain Bolt's pace)
note: Speed-record testbed; evolved into WildCat

name: LS3
desc: The Legged Squad Support System (also called AlphaDog), a militarised, ruggedised evolution of BigDog developed with DARPA and the US Marine Corps. Designed as a robotic pack mule to carry gear alongside soldiers over rough terrain, it could haul 181 kg for 32 km, follow a human leader and respond to voice commands, though the program was ultimately shelved.

name: HyQ
desc: The Italian Institute of Technology's pioneering hydraulically-actuated, torque-controlled research quadruped, developed by the Dynamic Legged Systems lab. Built to study fast, versatile and robust locomotion, HyQ demonstrated dynamic trotting, jumping and rough-terrain walking and seeded the later HyQReal platform.
note: Europe's landmark hydraulic quadruped — HyQ2Max/HyQReal successors (HyQReal towed a 3-tonne plane, 2019)

name: HyQReal
desc: IIT's larger, ruggedised electro-hydraulic quadruped, protected by an aluminium roll cage and a Kevlar, glass-fibre and plastic skin with high-traction rubber feet. Powered by a 48 V battery driving four electric motors coupled to four hydraulic pumps, it famously demonstrated its power by pulling a Piaggio P180 Avanti passenger aircraft.
actuator_type: Electro-hydraulic (4 electric motors driving 4 hydraulic pumps)

name: Solo 12
desc: Fully open-source (hardware + software) 12-DoF torque-controlled quadruped from the Max Planck / NYU Open Dynamic Robot Initiative — 3D-printable, ~2.5 kg, built so any lab can replicate cutting-edge legged research.
note: Fully open-source lab platform — buildable from published plans

name: Doggo
desc: An open-source, quasi-direct-drive quadruped from Stanford Student Robotics, designed as an accessible platform for legged-robot research. Presented at ICRA 2019, it holds a record for vertical jumping agility — jumping roughly twice as high as prior quadrupeds — while costing under $3,000 to build with only hand tools.
achievements: Record vertical jump agility for its size (quasi-direct-drive)
note: Student-built open-source milestone

name: ANYmal B
desc: The research-generation ANYmal, developed at ETH Zurich's Robotic Systems Lab and commercialised by ANYbotics. Driven by torque-controllable ANYdrive series-elastic actuators, it walks, trots, climbs stairs and recovers from falls, and served as the foundation for the later industrial ANYmal C/D/X inspection systems.

name: MagicDog Y1
desc: MagicLab's industrial flagship quadruped: IP67 aviation-grade body carrying 45 kg dynamically (150 kg standing) at up to 6 m/s, climbing 60 cm obstacles, 25 cm stairs and 45° slopes, with 3D LiDAR + dual depth + dual optical perception, centimeter positioning, hot-swap batteries and modular payload expansion for inspection and logistics.
note: Per-model specs sparse — verified platform only

name: Midnight
desc: Archer's piloted four-passenger eVTOL air taxi in FAA certification: 12 tilt-propellers, ~160 km range, 240 km/h cruise, designed for rapid back-to-back urban hops with minimal charge between flights.

name: Generation 6
desc: Boeing-backed Wisk's self-flying four-seat air taxi — the first candidate for autonomous, uncrewed passenger eVTOL flight in the US, with human supervisors on the ground.

name: ALIA
desc: An all-electric utility aircraft from BETA Technologies (Burlington, Vermont; NYSE-listed 2025). The flagship ALIA A250 eVTOL uses four top-mounted lift rotors plus a single rear pusher motor and a 50 ft (15 m) arctic-tern-inspired wing to combine vertical take-off with efficient wing-borne cruise, carrying five passengers or cargo up to 250 nmi (460 km) at 170 mph, recharging in under an hour. Distributed electric propulsion provides fail-safe redundancy, and BETA claims ~$17 of electricity to fly 150 miles versus ~$700 in jet fuel. Sister model CX300 is a conventional-take-off (eCTOL) variant on the same airframe (~336 nmi range, Garmin G3000 avionics), and an unmanned hybrid MV250 is in development. Orders from UPS, Bristow, Air New Zealand, Metro Aviation and United Therapeutics.
certification: FAA (in process); USAF AFWERX Agility Prime

name: VX4
desc: British four-passenger-plus-pilot eVTOL prototype: eight tilt-rotors, ~160 km range target at up to 240 km/h, backed by pre-orders from airlines and lessors.

name: Lilium Jet
desc: The 36-ducted-fan seven-seat eVTOL jet that pursued regional electric flight — a landmark program that flew full-scale demonstrators before Lilium's insolvency ended operations in 2025.

name: AeroHT X2
desc: A two-seat manned electric vertical-take-off aircraft from XPeng AeroHT (the flying-car affiliate of Chinese automaker XPeng), publicly flown in Dubai in 2022. The Voyager X2 is a closed-cockpit octacopter — eight rotors in a distributed-electric layout for stability and fail-safe redundancy — built around a lightweight carbon-fibre structure. It weighs about 560 kg empty, cruises around 130 km/h at low altitude (up to ~1,000 m), and offers roughly 35 minutes of flight. Sensing combines LiDAR, radar and ultrasonics with AI obstacle avoidance, and safety features include multi-rotor redundancy and a ballistic parachute. It's an early step in XPeng AeroHT's push toward a road-and-air 'flying car'.

name: FlyCart 30
desc: DJI's first delivery drone: carries 30 kg (dual-battery) or 40 kg (single-battery) up to 16 km loaded, at 20 m/s, with a 20 m winch system, dual radar + vision sensing and O3 transmission — bringing DJI reliability to heavy-lift logistics.

name: Chaparral
desc: An autonomous, hybrid-electric 'lift + cruise' VTOL cargo aircraft from San Francisco's Elroy Air, built to move freight to places without runways or airports. The Chaparral C1 carries 300-500 lb (136-227 kg) up to ~300 miles at roughly 125 knots, using twelve electric motors (eight for vertical lift, four for forward cruise) fed by a turbogenerator-battery architecture - a turbine tops up the batteries in flight, and the C1 was the world's first turbogenerator-hybrid hVTOL to fly (Nov 2023), completing its first point-to-point delivery in Dec 2025. Its full carbon-composite airframe rides fixed quadricycle gear that straddles a detachable modular cargo pod; the aircraft autonomously picks up and drops pods (express, heavy, humanitarian air-drop, climate-controlled/medical, ISR), creating a 'conveyor belt through the sky', and packs into a 40 ft container or C-130. It carries a backlog of ~1,500 preorders (~$3B) from FedEx, Bristow, LCI, AYR Logistics and the USAF, with Kratos as exclusive US manufacturer targeting 2026 production.
pod_types: Express, heavy, humanitarian air-drop, climate/medical, ISR
customers: FedEx, Bristow, LCI, AYR Logistics, USAF

name: Black Swan
desc: The flagship of Dronamics — the world's first cargo drone airline (founded 2014 by the Rangelov brothers, Sofia/London). The Black Swan is a clean-sheet, remotely-piloted fixed-wing cargo aircraft about the size of a two-seat Cessna, carrying 350 kg (3.5 m3) up to 2,500 km at up to 200 km/h, and taking off from ~400 m unpaved strips. Built predominantly from carbon fibre and powered by a Rotax propeller engine on sustainable fuel (with hydrogen planned), it targets 'middle-mile' same-day cargo — up to 80% faster, 50% cheaper and 60% lower-emission than airfreight. It was the first large UAV to hold an EU drone-airline license (LUC) and carries IATA/ICAO codes; a defence ISR variant adds a Hensoldt PrecISR payload.
certification: EU LUC drone-airline license; IATA/ICAO codes

name: RDST Longtail
desc: A ready-to-fly, second-generation commercial delivery drone from A2Z Drone Delivery (Los Angeles, with a test base outside Shanghai). The RDST Longtail is a rugged hexacopter with a factory-integrated RDS2 winch that lowers packages from ~30 m altitude — keeping spinning rotors away from people and property — and auto-releases the shipper's own boxes or bags (up to 5 kg) without a recipient on site. Built from carbon fibre and aluminium, it weighs 16 kg, meets the FAA 55-lb max-takeoff limit (24.95 kg MTOW), cruises at 20 m/s and carries a 5 kg payload up to 11 km (26 km unladen on the Premium). The rainproof Premium adds a quick-release 12S battery and centimetre-level RTK; both run the A2Z QGC (QGroundControl) station for pre-planned automated missions and are Remote ID compliant.

name: MQ-9 Reaper
desc: General Atomics' medium-altitude, long-endurance 'hunter-killer' - the first UAV engineered from the start for persistent strike as well as reconnaissance, and a backbone of US and allied airpower. A big evolution of the Predator, its carbon-composite, high-aspect-ratio (~20:1) 20 m wing (79 ft / 24 m on the MQ-9B) is driven by a 900 shp Honeywell TPE331-10GD turboprop, giving ~480 km/h top speed and 27 hours of ISR endurance (34+ on Extended Range) up to 50,000 ft, with ~1,850 km range. Empty weight is ~2,223 kg against a ~4,760 kg max takeoff weight, carrying up to ~1,700 kg of payload (360 kg internal plus 1,400 kg external across seven hardpoints). It fields an MTS-B EO/IR turret, synthetic aperture radar and a laser rangefinder/designator, relaying data over satellite links to a ground control station with triple-redundant avionics, and can employ precision-guided munitions (Hellfire-class missiles plus laser- and GPS-guided bombs). First flown in 2001 and operational since 2007 (~200+ built), it serves the USAF, DHS, NASA and allies including the UK, Italy, France, Spain, the Netherlands and Japan, with SkyGuardian/SeaGuardian maritime variants.
endurance: 27 h ISR (34 h ER); ~14 h with weapons
sensors: MTS-B EO/IR, SAR, laser designator, nose camera
operators: USAF, DHS, NASA, UK, Italy, France, Spain, Netherlands, Japan

name: MQ-1 Predator
desc: General Atomics' pioneering medium-altitude, long-endurance drone - the aircraft that defined armed ISR. Evolved from Abraham Karem's Amber/Gnat, the Predator entered US service in the mid-1990s as the RQ-1 reconnaissance platform and later, as the armed MQ-1, became the archetype of the persistent hunter-killer UAV. A composite, mid-wing pusher (48.7 ft / 14.8 m span, 8.2 m long, ~1,020 kg max takeoff weight) powered by a turbocharged Rotax 914 piston engine, it loitered 14-24 hours at up to ~25,000 ft with a ~1,250 km operational range, cruising around 135 km/h. It carried the AN/AAS-52 Multi-spectral Targeting System (EO/IR), synthetic aperture radar and a nose camera, relaying full-motion video over a satellite datalink to a ground station, and could mount precision-guided munitions on two hardpoints. Roughly 360 were built (unit cost ~$4M); the USAF retired the type from front-line service in 2018, though its lineage continues in the MQ-1C Gray Eagle and MQ-9 Reaper.

name: Bayraktar TB2
desc: Baykar's medium-altitude, long-endurance armed drone and the aircraft that put Turkey on the global UCAV map. A twin-boom design with an inverted-V tail, a straight high-aspect-ratio 12 m wing and a rear pusher prop, its carbon-composite airframe (6.5 m long, ~650 kg max takeoff weight) is driven by a 100 hp Rotax piston engine for 27 hours of endurance (it holds a 27h 3m record) at up to ~18,000-27,000 ft. It cruises around 130 km/h (top speed ~222 km/h), flies fully autonomously - including taxi, takeoff and landing - on a triple-redundant autopilot, and carries a nose EO/IR turret with laser designator (optional AESA radar) plus up to 150 kg of precision-guided munitions across four hardpoints. Combat-proven in conflicts from Nagorno-Karabakh to Ukraine, Libya and Syria, it has been exported to more than 20 countries with 355+ built.
config: Twin-boom, inverted-V tail, pusher prop (carbon composite)

name: Akıncı
desc: Baykar's flagship high-altitude, long-endurance unmanned combat aircraft (Bayraktar Akinci), a much larger sibling to the TB2. It's a twin-turboprop design - typically 450 hp AI-450T engines (with PD-170 and TP-395 variants) - spanning about 20 m with a ~12.2 m length and ~5,500 kg max takeoff weight, able to carry roughly 1,350 kg of payload across six hardpoints (internal and external). Published figures give it about 40,000 ft service ceiling, 24+ hours of endurance and ~361 km/h top speed. It runs AI-supported, triple-redundant avionics with satellite (beyond-line-of-sight) datalinks, can mount an AESA radar and EO/IR sensors, and carries precision-guided munitions and stand-off missiles for combined ISR and strike roles. In service with Turkey and exported to several operators.
engine: 2x turboprop (AI-450T 450 hp each; PD-170 / TP-395 variants)

name: RQ-4 Global Hawk
desc: Northrop Grumman's high-altitude, long-endurance strategic reconnaissance drone - the military's 'eye in the sky' that took over much of the U-2's mission. Powered by a single Rolls-Royce AE 3007H turbofan, the carbon-composite airframe with its very high-aspect-ratio wing and V-tail (RQ-4B: 39.9 m span, 14.5 m long, ~14,600 kg max takeoff weight) climbs above 60,000 ft and loiters 32-34+ hours (a record 33.1 h), ranging some 22,800 km at up to ~629 km/h. It carries a wide-area multi-sensor suite - synthetic aperture radar with ground-moving-target indication, EO/IR imaging and signals intelligence - relayed to ground stations over a Ku-band SATCOM link, and is unarmed. First flown in 1998 and in USAF service since 2001 (~50 built, ~$131M each), it spawned the RQ-4A/B, the NATO RQ-4D Phoenix, the German EuroHawk and the US Navy's maritime MQ-4C Triton.
operators: USAF, NATO, Germany, Japan, South Korea

name: ScanEagle
desc: A small, long-endurance ISR drone from Insitu (a Boeing subsidiary), derived from the commercial SeaScan fish-spotting UAV and in service since the mid-2000s. Its composite, high-aspect-ratio flying wing (3.1 m span, ~1.7 m long, ~26.5 kg) rides a small ~1.1 kW two-stroke, heavy-fuel-capable piston engine driving a pusher prop, giving 18-24 hours of endurance (a Block D set a 22h 8m record) at ~90 km/h cruise up to ~19,500 ft, with a 100 km line-of-sight datalink and SATCOM for beyond-line-of-sight work. It needs no runway: a pneumatic 'SuperWedge' catapult launches it and the patented 'SkyHook' wingtip-capture recovers it (an optional FLARES kit adds VTOL). It carries a stabilized EO/IR turret plus modular payloads (NanoSAR radar, ViDAR wide-area optics, laser targeting). Battle-proven with over 1.3 million operational hours since 2004 across US and allied forces (Australia, Canada, Poland, Brazil and more), it has flown ScanEagle 1, 2 and 3 variants.
recovery: SkyHook wingtip capture; FLARES VTOL kit
sensors: Stabilized EO/IR turret; NanoSAR, ViDAR, laser targeting (modular)

name: Switchblade 600
desc: AeroVironment's anti-armor loitering munition: tube-launched with ~40 km reach and ~40 minutes of loiter, carrying a Javelin-class warhead with wave-off and re-commit capability.

name: JUMP 20
desc: A runway-independent VTOL fixed-wing medium (Group 3) UAS for persistent multi-sensor ISR, derived from the Arcturus T-20 (AeroVironment acquired Arcturus in 2021). Four boom-mounted electric rotors handle vertical takeoff and landing while a heavy-fuel/MOGAS EFI engine drives efficient forward cruise, so it needs no runway or launcher and sets up in under 30-60 minutes with a two-person crew. It's 2.9 m long with a 5.7 m wingspan and ~97.5 kg max takeoff weight, carries up to 13.6 kg of payload (typically a gyro-stabilized EO/IR gimbal such as the TASE 400 series with onboard tracking), and delivers 13-14+ hours of endurance, a 185 km link range with BLOS capability, ~93 km/h cruise and a 17,000 ft ceiling. A Piccolo autopilot and modular open-systems (STANAG, payload/radio-agnostic) architecture make it highly configurable. The US Army picked it as FTUAS Increment 1 (2022, replacing the RQ-7 Shadow); it also serves Taiwan's Coast Guard, Mexico's Navy and Ukraine. A marinized JUMP 20-X variant adds autonomous shipboard operations.
config: VTOL fixed-wing (4 lift rotors + cruise engine)
propulsion: Heavy-fuel/MOGAS EFI engine (cruise) + 4 electric lift rotors
operators: US Army FTUAS Inc.1; Taiwan CGA; Mexico Navy; Ukraine

name: XQ-58 Valkyrie
desc: Kratos's low-cost, stealthy 'attritable' unmanned combat aircraft, developed for the US Air Force Research Laboratory's Low-Cost Attritable Strike Demonstrator program and designed to fly as a loyal wingman to crewed fighters (F-35, F-22, F-15EX, F/A-18). A trapezoidal, chined fuselage with a V-tail and S-shaped intake gives it a low radar signature; it's ~9.1 m long with an 8.2 m wingspan and ~2,948 kg max launch weight, powered by a single Williams FJ33 turbofan for high-subsonic speed (cruise Mach 0.72, up to ~Mach 0.85) out beyond 5,500 km at up to 45,000 ft. It's fully runway-independent - rocket-assisted rail launch and parachute/airbag recovery, with trolley- and landing-gear variants - and can launch from ships, containers or trucks. It carries ~272 kg internally plus wing stations, has released a smaller ALTIUS-600 drone from its bay, and flies under Skyborg AI autonomy. First flew March 2019; unit cost ~$4-6M (target sub-$2M at scale), producible at 250-500/year. The USMC selected it (with Northrop) for its first CCA in 2026; an electronic-attack MQ-58B and an Airbus/Bundeswehr variant are in work.
launch: Runway-independent: rocket/rail + parachute recovery (trolley & gear variants)
program: AFRL LCASD; USMC CCA (2026); Airbus / Bundeswehr

name: X-47B
desc: Northrop Grumman's carrier-based unmanned combat air vehicle technology demonstrator, built for the US Navy's UCAS-D program to prove that a stealthy, tailless jet could operate autonomously from an aircraft carrier. A B-2-inspired blended-wing-body flying wing powered by a single Pratt & Whitney F100-220U turbofan, it spans 18.9 m (folding to 9.4 m for the deck), is 11.6 m long, and has a ~20,185 kg max takeoff weight. It flew at high-subsonic speed (~Mach 0.9) out beyond 3,900 km at up to ~40,000 ft, with two internal bays rated for ~2,040 kg (the demonstrators flew unarmed) and EO/IR, SAR and ESM sensors under GPS/vision-based semi-autonomous control. Two were built (Salty Dog 501/502); first flight February 2011. It logged aviation firsts - the first UAV carrier catapult launch and autonomous arrested carrier landing (2013) and the first fully autonomous aerial refueling (2015) - before the test program concluded and it retired, serving as the basis for later carrier-UAV efforts (UCLASS/MQ-25).
firsts: First UAV carrier catapult launch + autonomous arrested landing (2013); first autonomous aerial refuel (2015)
program: US Navy UCAS-D (basis for UCLASS / MQ-25)

name: MQ-25 Stingray
desc: The U.S. Navy's first carrier-based unmanned aircraft — a Boeing-built autonomous aerial-refueling tanker drone whose primary job is to offload fuel to F/A-18 Super Hornets (via a wing-mounted buddy refueling store), freeing fighters from the tanking role, with a secondary ISR mission through a retractable EO/IR sensor turret. It has a ~75 ft (22.9 m) wingspan, a Rolls-Royce AE 3007N turbofan fed by a low-observable top-mounted flush inlet, and flies fully autonomously (taxi, take-off, maneuver, land) under the MD-5 Ground Control Station. A T1 demonstrator first flew in 2019 and the production-representative MQ-25A made its maiden flight in 2026; the Navy plans 76 aircraft with IOC targeted for 2026.

name: MQ-28 Ghost Bat
desc: Australia's Boeing-built collaborative combat aircraft — the first military aircraft designed and built in Australia in over 50 years, flying AI-teaming missions alongside crewed fighters with a 3,700 km range.

name: Fury (YFQ-44A)
desc: Anduril's high-performance autonomous air vehicle (selected as the USAF's YFQ-44A CCA candidate): a jet-powered fighter-class drone built around the Lattice autonomy stack for manned-unmanned teaming.

name: P100 Pro
desc: XAG's flagship agri drone (DJI Agras' main rival): 50 kg spray/spread capacity with RevoSpray 3 atomization, RealTerra RTK terrain following and fully autonomous field operations.

name: AG-272
desc: A US-built eight-rotor heavy-lift agricultural spray drone from Hylio (Richmond/Houston, Texas), designed for large North American acreage with full operator control over hardware and data (no proprietary lock-in). It carries an 18-gallon (68.2 L) spray tank with a 40 ft (12.2 m) swath and 15 L/min flow through industry-standard TeeJet nozzles, covering ~50 acres/hour. The airframe weighs 53 kg empty with a 181 kg max takeoff weight and 272 kg combined thrust, running two 51.8 V LiPo packs (2,176 Wh) for 10–15 min flights and ~25–30 min recharge. Wide-angle radar gives near-spherical obstacle detection, and one operator can run up to three drones via the ruggedized GroundLink controller (13.3-inch Windows tablet). FAA Part 137 and NDAA compliant, modular and field-serviceable.

name: Airpeak S1
desc: Sony's first professional drone (announced June 2021) and the world's smallest quadcopter able to carry a full-frame Sony Alpha mirrorless camera. Its four 17-inch props and Sony-designed brushless motors give it up to 55.9 mph (25 m/s) top speed, 0-50 mph in 3.5 s, 180 deg/s angular velocity, a 55-degree attitude angle and wind resistance to 44.7 mph. It flies ~22 minutes unloaded (about 12 with a heavy payload) on hot-swappable batteries and lifts a camera-plus-gimbal payload up to 2.5 kg (Gremsy T3 or GBL-PX1 gimbals, sold separately), compatible with Alpha bodies from the a7S/FX3 to the 8K a1. Five directional stereo cameras plus two IR range sensors feed Sony's Vision Sensing Processor for obstacle avoidance and GNSS-denied positioning; retractable landing gear keeps the shot clear, and a nose FPV camera, Airpeak Flight (iOS) app and cloud-based Airpeak Base enable Mission/Repeat automated flight and dual-operator control. Body-only price around $9,000.
camera_compat: Sony Alpha full-frame (a7S / FX3 / a7R / a9 / a1 8K)

name: X8 Pro
desc: A folding consumer camera drone from FIMI (Xiaomi ecosystem), positioned as a value DJI alternative. It carries a 1/1.3-inch 48 MP CMOS sensor (f/1.7, dual native ISO, HDR) on a 3-axis mechanical gimbal shooting 4K/30fps, and folds to 204 x 106 x 73 mm at ~780 g. FIMI's RokLink 4.0 transmission reaches up to 15 km with ~130 ms latency, tri-directional dual-camera obstacle sensing detects out to 15 m, and flight time runs 37 min (Intelligent Flight Battery) or up to 47 min with the Battery Plus. Multi-GNSS (GPS/Galileo/BeiDou/GLONASS), Grade-7 wind resistance, Remote ID and rain/snow resistance round it out, plus optional megaphone and release-and-drop payload modules.

name: X1 Pro Max
desc: Zero Zero Robotics' flagship pocket selfie drone: 8K/30fps video at just ~192 g, palm take-off, fully enclosed props and AI subject tracking — the high end of the X1 family.

name: Voliro T
desc: A purpose-built industrial-inspection drone from Voliro (an ETH Zurich spin-off) that doesn't just fly and see — it touches. Thrust-vectoring tiltable rotors give true omnidirectional (6-DoF) freedom and up to ±90-degree tilt, letting it press against vertical walls, ceilings and curved surfaces with up to 30 N of stable force (plus several Nm of torque) to 'seat' non-destructive-testing sensors for reliable coupling. Assisted autonomy handles the approach-and-touch phase even in GPS-denied spaces like tanks and boilers. Six interchangeable NDT payloads — EMAT, ultrasonic thickness, dry-film coating, pulsed-eddy-current, lightning-protection and a flammable-gas sensor — cover most inspection jobs, with live A-Scan in the Voliro app, hot-swappable self-heating batteries, and a subscription business model.

name: Agras T70
desc: DJI Agriculture's high-capacity 2025 workhorse, a foldable coaxial-rotor drone that sprays, spreads and lifts. The base T70 carries a 50 L spray tank (the uprated T70P a 70 L tank at up to 129.8 kg max takeoff weight), both sharing a 100 L granule hopper that spreads at up to 400 kg/min over a 10 m width, plus a 65 kg cargo-lift mode on a 10-15 m rope. Dual atomizing centrifugal nozzles push up to 40 L/min across a 4-11 m spray width with 50-500 um droplets. Safety System 3.0 fuses millimetre-wave radar with a Tri-Vision camera array for 360-degree obstacle avoidance and terrain-following out to 60 m, and RTK gives +/-1 cm positioning. A carbon-fibre airframe on 62-inch props, DB1580 (30,000 mAh / 52 V) batteries that recharge in 7-9 minutes, a night FPV camera and the TKPL2 7-inch controller round it out; validated over 700 hours of reliability testing.
obstacle_avoidance: Safety System 3.0: mmWave radar + Tri-Vision, 360, 60 m

name: Tumbller Self-Balancing Robot
desc: ELEGOO's self-balancing, two-wheeled Arduino robot car - a hands-on STEM kit that teaches PID control, sensor fusion and programming. Built on an Arduino Nano with an MPU6050 6-axis IMU and a TB6612FNG motor driver, it balances itself upright on two wheels: press the command key and it tilts forward, press again and it stands back up, holding balance on its own (it stops the wheels once tilted beyond about 27 degrees). An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor and dual side infrared sensors give it obstacle avoidance and auto-follow, and it adds a 'bouncing' mode plus six switchable RGB LED light effects. It's controlled by IR remote or over Bluetooth from the ELEGOO BLE Tool app (iOS/Android), and is fully Arduino-IDE compatible so learners can modify the code and wire in extra sensors via the reserved pins. Aimed at ages 12+, around $85.
control: IR remote + ELEGOO BLE Tool app (iOS/Android)
features: Self-balancing, auto-follow, obstacle avoidance, bouncing mode, 6 RGB LED effects

name: Conqueror Robot Tank Kit
desc: ELEGOO's premium tracked robot tank - a metal-chassis STEM kit built around an Arduino UNO R3 plus an ESP32-WROVER Wi-Fi module and an OV2640 camera for first-person (FPV) driving streamed live to a phone. The camera sits on a two-degree-of-freedom gimbal with up to 180-degree horizontal control, and the stainless-steel tracked drive tackles rough surfaces. It offers five interactive modes - FPV driving, infrared remote control, obstacle avoidance, line tracking and auto-follow - so learners explore sensors, motor control, navigation logic and wireless communication on one platform. Programming steps up from block-based coding in the ELEGOO app to text-based projects in the Arduino IDE, with plug-in wiring and included tools for a rewarding metal DIY build. Aimed at ages 8+, around $100.
modes: FPV, IR remote, obstacle avoidance, line tracking, auto-follow (5)

name: Smart Robot Car Kit V3.0 Plus
desc: The previous-generation flagship of ELEGOO's Smart Robot Car line and still widely sold - a four-wheel-drive Arduino robot car designed as an all-in-one introduction to programming, electronics assembly and robotics. Built on an Arduino UNO R3 with a sensor shield, it ships with 24 kinds of module parts (obstacle-avoidance ultrasonic, line-tracking infrared, IR remote and more) and supports auto-go, IR control, obstacle-avoidance and line-tracking modes. All module interfaces use keyed XH2.54 connectors to make assembly easier and reduce wiring errors, and it can be driven by IR remote or via a Bluetooth app on Android/iOS. Fully Arduino-IDE compatible for custom code. Superseded by the Smart Robot Car Kit V4.0; around $70.
modes: Auto-go, IR control, obstacle avoidance, line tracking

name: OwlBot Tank Kit
desc: The tracked-tank member of ELEGOO's OwlBot beginner line - a friendly, owl-themed STEM robot aimed at younger learners moving into block-based coding. Like its OwlBot car sibling it pairs approachable hardware with the ElegooKit app, where children program the robot's lights, sounds, sensors and movement using block-based coding before graduating to text-based programming. desc: The Flexiv Rizon 4 is the world's first adaptive robot — unveiled at Hannover Messe in April 2019 — and the founding model of Flexiv's Rizon series. Unlike position-controlled cobots, the Rizon 4 is built around force control: torque sensors in all seven axes give it whole-body force sensitivity (0.1 N sensing accuracy, up to 200 N TCP force), letting it perform contact-rich tasks like polishing, insertion and assembly while tolerating positional uncertainty that would defeat conventional arms. Its human-arm-inspired 7-DoF kinematics (4 kg payload, 876 mm reach, ±0.05 mm ISO 9283 repeatability, 20 kg mass) keep an optimised force-control posture through the workspace, and the IP65 body mounts at any angle including on AMR/AGV platforms. Built to ISO 13849 PL=d with dual-channel redundancy and CE & ETL certified, it runs from the compact Hesper controller and is programmed via Flexiv Elements drag-and-drop primitives or the C++/Python RDK. Founded by Stanford robotics researchers, Flexiv positioned the Rizon 4 as a third robot category beyond industrial and collaborative arms.

desc: The Kinova Gen3 lite is the compact, cost-efficient member of Kinova's ultra-lightweight arm family — a 6-axis arm at just 5.4 kg with a 0.5 kg payload, 760 mm reach and an integrated 2-finger adaptive gripper included, aimed squarely at professional academic education and cost-sensitive research. desc: Honda's P1, developed in 1993, was the first of Honda's 'P' (Prototype) series — a large 1,915 mm, 175 kg experimental platform with 30 DOF that attached legs to a torso with two arms capable of basic tasks. Honda kept P1's existence secret until it announced the P2 in 1996. It was the tethered testbed on which Honda established the stable bipedal walking that led to P2, P3 and ultimately ASIMO.
